1.pericope_label: As snow in summer, and as rain in harvest, so honour is not seemly for a fool... Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he be wise in his own conceit

schools.summary: Delitzsch and Ellicott both move the harm of misplaced honour from the community to the man honoured, who will use it unjustly and be confirmed in the good opinion he already holds; Delitzsch also reports and rejects an attempt to reverse whip and bridle in the third verse, and distinguishes the two senses of according to his folly that reconcile the fourth verse with the fifth.

Gill contributes the local colour — untimely rain as a marvel in that climate, the swallow named in Hebrew from its liberty, the horse dull of going — and holds that a fool is sometimes not to be answered at all, and never in his own virulent manner.

Clarke states the plain incongruity of the first verse, has the undeserved curse flutter about a neighbourhood and vanish like a migrant bird, and imports Warburton's distinction that the defender of religion must not copy the insulter's sophistry, buffoonery and scurrility, but must confute him out of his own principles; Wesley compresses the paired commands into two glosses, imitating folly against supplying what folly requires.

Henry reads the group politically and pastorally at once: preferment for the worthless as a disorder in the state, cursing as the impotent malice of the powerful, sinners so far sunk that only force or fear governs them, and the scripture's apparent self-contradiction as a piece of practical wisdom about when to speak.

debates.question: Whom does honour given to a fool chiefly damage?

positions.view: The fool himself; it strengthens his folly, and he draws false conclusions from it.
The commonwealth; power in such hands discourages virtue and countenances wickedness.
Neither is pressed; the point is simply that the thing is out of season.

debates.question: How are the two opposite commands about answering a fool reconciled?

positions.view: The phrase bears two senses: entertaining the foolish premise, which levels you with him, and giving folly what it deserves in a short sharp reply.
They divide by occasion: never copy his manner, but answer when silence would be taken for weakness.
They divide by method: do not imitate his sophistry and scurrility, but do confute him out of his own principles.
Silence is generally best, on the pattern of Christ, who put by questions that should not have been asked.

outliers.note: Answers a proposed emendation of the third verse by appeal to a figure of speech in which whip and bridle each belong to both animals, and settles the order on rhythmical grounds.
Reports a marginal Hebrew reading at the second verse which substitutes to him for not, so that the causeless curse returns upon its author.

themes: As snow in summer, and as rain in harvest, so honour is not seemly for a fool.
As the bird by wandering, as the swallow by flying, so the curse causeless shall not come.
A whip for the horse, a bridle for the ass, and a rod for the fool’s back.
Answer not a fool according to his folly, lest thou also be like unto him.
Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he be wise in his own conceit.

6.pericope_label: He that sendeth a message by the hand of a fool cutteth off the feet, and drinketh damage... The great God that formed all things both rewardeth the fool, and rewardeth transgressors

schools.summary: Delitzsch carries the philological weight of the section — the sender who cuts off his own legs, the disputed opening word of the seventh verse, the defence of the sling against rival renderings, the thorn that cannot be said to grow in a hand — and declares the tenth verse more obscure than anything before it, revocalizing to obtain a sense; Ellicott glosses each figure briefly and rejects the received rendering of the tenth verse as unsustainable Hebrew.

Gill supplies the alternatives rather than choosing among them, especially at the sling, where he offers a stone tied fast, a jewel among the rubble heaped over a criminal, and a common stone wrapped in purple.

Clarke works through older English and Latin versions, following the sling into a heap of money, a gallows and a wayside heap sacred to Mercury, and locates the ambiguity of the tenth verse in a single word that may name God or a great man; Wesley adds short glosses, that the messenger is bidden to go without legs and that drinking in scripture means receiving in quantity.

Henry stays with conduct: what actually happens to a badly carried message, how a master is judged by his messenger, and the two readings of the tenth verse as either the equity of God repaying ignorance and presumption differently or the tyranny of a great man who hires fools to grieve everyone.

debates.question: Whose feet are cut off in the sixth verse?

positions.view: The sender's own; he meant to borrow the messenger's legs and has lost his own.
The messenger's; he might as well have crippled the man he sends.

debates.question: What does the tenth verse say?

positions.view: The received English is unsustainable; read instead that a master gets everything done himself while a fool hires any passer-by.
The text is corrupt or obscure beyond the versions' reach; revocalized, the reward and the hirer of the fool pass away.
Both English readings are tenable, since one word may mean either the great God or a great man.
The plain sense stands: the recompense deserved will certainly be given.

outliers.note: Pursues the sling through the versions as far as the Latin, which has the man casting a stone onto a heap sacred to Mercury, god of highways.
Opens his note on the tenth verse by declaring it more obscure than everything read so far, and dismisses the Syriac solution — a drunken man sailing over the sea — as meaningless.

themes: He that sendeth a message by the hand of a fool cutteth off the feet, and drinketh damage.
The legs of the lame are not equal: so is a parable in the mouth of fools.
As he that bindeth a stone in a sling, so is he that giveth honour to a fool.
As a thorn goeth up into the hand of a drunkard, so is a parable in the mouth of fools.
The great God that formed all things both rewardeth the fool, and rewardeth transgressors.

11.pericope_label: As a dog returneth to his vomit, so a fool returneth to his folly... The sluggard is wiser in his own conceit than seven men that can render a reason

schools.summary: Delitzsch supplies the natural history and the philology — that dogs do return to their vomit, that the beast in the sluggard's excuse is a lion and not a jackal, that the door never leaves the narrow arc allowed it, that the sluggard's name means one glued to his place — and denies any necessary link between sloth and conceit while supplying the sluggard's own reasoning for the boast; Ellicott adds little beyond cross-references and one note on the compulsion of habit.

Gill measures the distance between what a man knows and what he thinks he knows, names the religious form of self-conceit, and calls the sluggard's claim to wisdom a contradiction in terms, since he will not use the means by which wisdom is got.
Clarke offers nothing here but pointers to his notes elsewhere; Wesley contributes a single line on the door, moved but not removed.

Henry supplies the moral psychology throughout: sin vomited under conviction and licked up again by a man convinced and never converted, the self-conceited pupil whom no teacher can reach, the sluggard who dreads not the lion but the road, and the professor hung on the two hinges of the world and the flesh.

debates.question: Why is the self-conceited man harder to help than the fool?

positions.view: Because the belief that no improvement is needed is itself the obstacle to improvement.
Because such a man is ignorant of himself, mistaking outward observance for righteousness and in some cases claiming perfection.
From a teacher's experience: those who think themselves wise cannot be instructed, and the sluggard is the worst case, taking his idleness for prudence.
The gospel supplies the illustration: those who had strayed returned at the preaching while those who supposed they needed nothing rejected the counsel.

outliers.note: Notes that the apostle who later quotes the proverb about the dog did not draw his wording from the Greek version, and elsewhere reconstructs the sluggard's argument that hard work ruins the health and that the cleverest are commonly cracked.
Contributes no exposition to this group at all, referring the reader to notes on other passages at both places where he appears.

themes: As a dog returneth to his vomit, so a fool returneth to his folly.
Seest thou a man wise in his own conceit? there is more hope of a fool than of him.
The slothful man saith, There is a lion in the way; a lion is in the streets.
As the door turneth upon his hinges, so doth the slothful upon his bed.
The slothful hideth his hand in his bosom; it grieveth him to bring it again to his mouth.
The sluggard is wiser in his own conceit than seven men that can render a reason.

17.pericope_label: He that passeth by, and meddleth with strife belonging not to him, is like one that taketh a dog by the ears... The words of a talebearer are as wounds, and they go down into the innermost parts of the belly

schools.summary: Delitzsch frames the section as caricatures recommending peace, objects to the syntax of the first verse, reports that the participle of the madman has no settled rendering among the old translators, distinguishes black coal from glowing coal, and renders the closing line not as wounds but as dainty morsels that glide down; Ellicott translates the meddler as one excited by the quarrel and explains the firebrands as arrows carrying blazing material.

Gill sharpens the meddler into a partisan who inflames what he interrupts, lists the possible senses of the madman's participle including feigned madness and concealment, and notes that the closing verse is a repetition gathered here by Hezekiah's men.

Clarke supplies the observations that the proverb about meddling holds most reliably in domestic quarrels, that this sort of sport has killed many reputations, and that the receiver of slander is as guilty as its carrier; Wesley reduces the first proverb to needless hazard and the last noun of the eighteenth verse to any instrument of death.

Henry provides the images that carry the section — the dog that cannot be held or released, the jest that must be repented in earnest, contention as a fire and tales as fireballs, and the talebearer's words as wounds beyond the reach of retraction.

debates.question: What are the words of the talebearer like?

positions.view: Wounds, deep and in the vitals, injuring the reputation of the absent and the charity of the hearer.
Dainty morsels, which glide down into the innermost parts — a comment on the hearer's appetite rather than the victim's injury.
The contentious man, who functions as fuel does, existing to heat what is already burning.
The talebearer, who ought to be expelled from every society, since old grievances die out when nobody renews them.
The listener as much as the carrier, slander being unable to spread unless somebody receives it.

outliers.note: Presses the guilt of the audience rather than the gossip, comparing the receiver of stolen goods, who was hanged with the thief.
Reports that the participle describing the madman has no traditional rendering whatever, the old versions giving malicious, testing, vainglorious, injurious and a spiritual successor.

themes: He that passeth by, and meddleth with strife belonging not to him, is like one that taketh a dog by the ears.
As a mad man who casteth firebrands, arrows, and death,
So is the man that deceiveth his neighbour, and saith, Am not I in sport?
Where no wood is, there the fire goeth out: so where there is no talebearer, the strife ceaseth.
As coals are to burning coals, and wood to fire; so is a contentious man to kindle strife.
The words of a talebearer are as wounds, and they go down into the innermost parts of the belly.

23.pericope_label: Burning lips and a wicked heart are like a potsherd covered with silver dross... A lying tongue hateth those that are afflicted by it; and a flattering mouth worketh ruin

schools.summary: Delitzsch identifies the silver dross as litharge used to glaze pottery, argues that the verb of the twenty-fourth verse can mean to make oneself unrecognisable as readily as to become known, traces the pit and the stone through several literatures, and rejects every proposed rescue of the last verse on the ground that the participle means bruised rather than bruising; Ellicott glosses the burning lips as burning with love over an evil heart and reads the twenty-sixth verse as a concession that hatred may hide for a time.

Gill sets out the alternatives at almost every point — malice or feigned love, the hater concealed or the hater exposed, hatred covered by deceit or covered in a desert place, four possible senses for the last verse — and generally declines to choose.

Clarke supplies the plated vessel whose outside is not even pure, the flat advice to let all such professions go for nothing, a Latin proverb on bad counsel recoiling upon its giver, and the observation that a man hates his victim in proportion to that victim's innocence; Wesley reads the burning lips as malice and adds short glosses elsewhere.

Henry works the section as a study of dissembled friendship, from the kindly words of biblical murderers through the caution against believing fair speech to the exposure that must come, and closes by ranking the flatterer who kisses and kills above the slanderer who declares war.

debates.question: What is the heat of the burning lips?

positions.view: Malice; a slanderous tongue, worthless as dross that imitates silver.
Feigned love; lips glowing with professed affection over a base heart, matching the glaze on cheap ware.
Either will do, but the second suits what follows.

debates.question: Does the hater in the twenty-fourth verse conceal himself or betray himself?

positions.view: He disguises himself; the verb bears the sense of making oneself unrecognisable, though every ancient translator read it the other way.
Both readings stand in the versions: he hides his grudge, or he is known by his lips, since he cannot forbear betraying himself.

outliers.note: Explains the last verse psychologically rather than lexically: an injurer hates his victim in proportion to the injury done and, strangely, to the victim's innocence, as a debtor cannot bear the sight of his creditor.
Argues that the stone of the twenty-seventh verse is rolled uphill, so that it returns on the roller's own head, and cites the French and Italian forms of the same proverb.

themes: Burning lips and a wicked heart are like a potsherd covered with silver dross.
He that hateth dissembleth with his lips, and layeth up deceit within him;
When he speaketh fair, believe him not: for there are seven abominations in his heart.
Whose hatred is covered by deceit, his wickedness shall be shewed before the whole congregation.
Whoso diggeth a pit shall fall therein: and he that rolleth a stone, it will return upon him.
A lying tongue hateth those that are afflicted by it; and a flattering mouth worketh ruin.
